def: Sheth and Sisodia's buyer-side view of the marketing mix: acceptability, affordability, accessibility and awareness.
Any paid, non-personal presentation of ideas, goods or services by an identified sponsor.
A response model: attention, interest, desire, action; usually credited to E. St. Elmo Lewis.
A way of profiling consumer lifestyle through activities, interests and opinions.
A learned predisposition to respond favourably or unfavourably toward a product, brand or idea.
The product level that adds services and benefits such as delivery, warranty and after-sales service.
Non-store retailing through unmanned machines that sell around the clock.
A name, term, sign, symbol or design, or a combination, that identifies a seller's goods and differentiates them from competitors'.
The added value a brand gives a product in customers' minds, shown in their perceptions, preferences and behaviour.
Using an established brand name to enter a new product category.
All the brands and brand lines a firm offers in a category or segment, each with a role such as flanker or prestige brand.
Keller's pyramid of brand building: salience, performance and imagery, judgements and feelings, and resonance.
Young and Rubicam's brand equity model with four pillars: energised differentiation, relevance, esteem and knowledge.
Robinson, Faris and Wind's classification of business purchases into straight rebuy, modified rebuy and new task.
Robinson, Faris and Wind's grid crossing the three buyclasses with eight stages (buyphases) of the industrial buying process.
Everyone involved in an organisational purchase: users, influencers, buyers, deciders and gatekeepers, with initiators and approvers.
Lauterborn's customer-side restatement of the 4Ps: customer solution, cost, convenience and communication.
Using a brand to enter a product category different from its original one.
A wholesaler, retailer, agent or broker that helps move a product from producer to consumer.
The rate at which customers stop doing business with a firm over a period.
Putting two or more established brand names on one product.
Discomfort after a purchase caused by doubt about the choice; ‘buyer's remorse’.
A decision rule in which a product must meet a minimum acceptable level on every attribute.
The basic benefit or need the customer is really buying.
Setting price by adding a standard mark-up to cost.
The present value of the profits a customer will bring over the whole relationship.
Demand for business goods that comes from demand for the consumer goods they help produce.
One-to-one communication designed to get an immediate, measurable response.
A retailer selling standard goods at low prices, with low margins and high volume.
A decision rule in which a product is accepted if it meets a high standard on any one key attribute.
The set of organisations, direct or through intermediaries, through which a product passes from producer to final consumer.
The brands a buyer actively considers when evaluating alternatives.
In social marketing, the idea that a behaviour change must offer benefits that outweigh its perceived costs.
Distribution through one or very few dealers in each area; typical of luxury and specialty goods.
Entering a foreign market by selling home-produced goods there, directly or through intermediaries.
Entering a foreign market by building or buying production facilities there: the highest risk and full control.
A lower-priced ‘fighter’ brand launched to protect a flagship brand from competitors.
A contractual system of outlets run under a franchisor's brand and system, for a fee.
A buying-centre member who controls the flow of information to the others.
Marketing environmentally sustainable products and practices.
Making false or exaggerated environmental claims about a product.
Unconventional, low-cost tactics designed to surprise audiences and create buzz.
Low-involvement buying where brands differ little, needing minimal decision-making; salt is the usual example.
The variability of service quality depending on who provides it, when, where and how.
Kotler and Keller's view of marketing as one connected system: relationship, integrated, internal and performance marketing.
Cooperation between unrelated firms at the same level of a channel to exploit an opportunity.
Peppers and Rogers' one-to-one marketing steps: identify, differentiate, interact, customise.
The process by which organisations establish needs and choose among products and suppliers for production, operations or resale.
The service characteristic that production and consumption happen together.
The service characteristic that it cannot be seen, touched or tried before purchase.
Coordinating all promotion tools to deliver one clear, consistent message.
Placing a product in as many outlets as possible; typical of convenience goods.
The employee-customer side of the service triangle, where the service is delivered.
Hiring, training and motivating employees to serve customers well.
Entering a foreign market in partnership with a local firm, sharing ownership, control and risk.
A traditional Indian neighbourhood store, now modernising with self-service, credit, home delivery and digital ordering.
A decision rule that compares brands on the most important attribute first.
Entering a foreign market by letting a local firm use a process, trademark or patent for a royalty.
A new item in an existing product category under the same brand name, such as a new flavour or size.
Aaker's levels of brand loyalty: switchers, habitual buyers, satisfied buyers with switching costs, brand likers, committed buyers.
Planning, implementing and controlling the physical flow of goods and information from origin to point of use, to meet customer needs at a profit; also called physical distribution.
Dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers with similar needs, characteristics or behaviour.
The philosophy that success comes from knowing target customers' needs and satisfying them better than competitors.
The controllable tools, product, price, place and promotion, that a firm blends to get the response it wants.
Levitt's term for defining a business by its product rather than by the need it serves.
A corporation owning several diversified retail brands and formats.
A business buying situation in which products, prices or suppliers are re-evaluated because needs have changed.
Launching new brands in an existing category to capture different segments.
The process of taking a product from idea generation to commercialisation, in eight steps.
A first-time organisational purchase needing extensive research and many decision-makers.
Focusing on a narrow, well-defined and often underserved group.
Selling to consumers outside fixed stores: direct selling, direct marketing, vending and buying services.
Setting the promotion budget by costing the tasks needed to reach defined objectives; the most logical method.
A store selling leftover, surplus or irregular branded goods below regular prices.
Treating each customer as a segment of one.
Launching at a low price to win market share quickly.
Marketing in which the advertiser pays only when a measurable action, such as a click, lead or sale, occurs.
The service characteristic that it cannot be stored; unused capacity is lost.
Seeking customers' consent before sending them marketing messages.
Face-to-face presentation by a salesperson to make sales and build relationships.
Attributes or benefits customers strongly associate with a brand and believe they could not find to the same extent in competitors.
Associations, not unique to the brand, that it needs to be credible in its category or to neutralise a rival's advantages.
Designing an offering and image to occupy a distinct, valued place in the target customer's mind.
A brand created and owned by a retailer or wholesaler; a store brand.
The stages a product's sales and profits pass through: introduction, growth, maturity and decline.
A group of closely related products made or sold by the same firm.
All the product lines and items a firm offers, measured by width, length, depth and consistency.
The blend of advertising, sales promotion, personal selling, public relations and direct marketing.
A preference for entering countries with a similar language, culture and legal system.
Pricing that works on perceptions, such as odd prices, reference prices and price as a signal of quality.
Promoting to final consumers so that they ask channel members for the product.
Promoting to channel members, who then promote to final buyers.
In media planning, how many people see an ad at least once, and how often the average person sees it.
Building long-term relationships with customers, employees and partners rather than focusing on single transactions.
Independent retailers who set up a joint buying organisation and run joint promotions.
Managing returns, recalls, repairs, recycling and excess stock back through the supply chain.
Advertising on many channels at the same time so the audience meets the message wherever it turns.
Marketing designed for rural consumers, often framed by availability, affordability, acceptability and awareness.
Short-term incentives to encourage trial or purchase, aimed at consumers, the trade or the sales force.
Distribution through more than one but fewer than all willing outlets; typical of shopping goods.
The links between company, employees and customers: internal, external and interactive marketing.
A model measuring the gap between expected and perceived service on five dimensions: reliability, assurance, tangibles, empathy, responsiveness.
Booms and Bitner's services mix: product, price, place, promotion, people, process and physical evidence.
Launching at a high price for buyers who value novelty, then lowering it over time.
Using marketing techniques to influence behaviour that benefits individuals and society.
The philosophy that a firm should serve both customers' wants and society's long-term well-being.
Entering many countries at the same time to gain first-mover advantage.
Segmentation, targeting and positioning: the sequence at the heart of marketing strategy.
A routine business purchase from an established supplier with little evaluation.
A brand formed by combining a new name with an existing brand name, as in Cadbury Dairy Milk Silk.
Managing the whole chain from procurement through manufacturing to delivery, across organisations.
Evaluating segments and choosing which to serve.
The tension between customer service level and total logistics cost: more of one usually means more of the other.
Persuading a customer to buy a higher-value version or an add-on.
The value that makes a product able to satisfy a want: form, place, time, possession or information utility.
The full set of benefits on which a brand is positioned and that it promises to deliver.
Setting price by the customer's perceived value rather than by cost.
Low-involvement buying where buyers switch among clearly different brands for variety.
A channel in which producer, wholesaler and retailer act as one unified system: corporate, contractual or administered.
Independent retailers organised by a wholesaler for group buying and common merchandising.
Entering foreign markets one at a time, in sequence, for controlled expansion and learning.
A model of organisational buying in which environmental, organisational, interpersonal and individual factors influence the buying centre.
An intermediary that buys in bulk from producers and resells to retailers or other businesses.
A direct channel in which the producer sells straight to the consumer.
The range between desired and adequate service within which variations in service go largely unnoticed.
